title: Nvidia Nears $6 Trillion on Record Highs and Biggest Buyback Ever
excerpt: Shares hit a record $239.11 as the AI chipmaker closes in on the first-ever $6 trillion market cap, powered by a $150 billion buyback and a $108 billion revenue outlook.
body:
• Nvidia shares closed at a record $239.11 on Oct. 5, pushing the AI chipmaker's market value to just shy of $5.8 trillion — within roughly $300 billion of becoming the first company ever worth $6 trillion.
  • The latest leg of the rally rests on two pillars: a robust revenue outlook — the company has guided to about $108 billion in current-quarter revenue — and a $150 billion increase to its share buyback, the largest repurchase authorization in corporate history, bringing total remaining buyback capacity to $235 billion.
  • The stock is up 28% in 2026, adding $1.2 trillion in market value and making Nvidia by far the biggest contributor to the S&P 500's 14% gain this year — even though it is still trailing the broader semiconductor sector, which is up about 86%.
  • What it means for you: Nvidia now accounts for roughly 7–8% of the S&P 500, so anyone holding a US index fund already owns it indirectly and feels its moves. Watch the next quarterly report against the $108 billion revenue guide, Morgan Stanley's reinstated top-pick call, and Fed rate decisions with the 10-year Treasury at a 24-year high of 5.3% — no action implied, just the data points that will move the stock.

Nvidia is on the verge of becoming the first company in history with a $6 trillion market capitalization, as investors rotate back into the artificial-intelligence chipmaker with fresh conviction.

The shares are at record highs after the company gave a robust revenue outlook and announced the biggest share buyback in history — a combination that has pushed the stock up 28% this year in a rally that has added $1.2 trillion to Nvidia's market value, bringing it to just shy of $5.8 trillion, according to Bloomberg. The stock touched an intraday record of $240.10 on Monday and closed at $239.11, up 2.2%, its first record close since May.

Two pillars: the outlook and the buyback

The immediate catalyst was the board's authorization of an additional $150 billion under its existing share-repurchase program, announced Sept. 28 — the largest single buyback in U.S. corporate history. With the new authorization, Nvidia's total remaining repurchase capacity stands at about $235 billion through fiscal 2028.

Chief Executive Jensen Huang said the move "reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead," and has previously described Nvidia as "the world's first and only growth value stock." Wall Street tends to like buybacks: they return cash to shareholders and reduce the share count, lifting earnings per share. Nvidia's repurchase stands out among Big Tech companies, which are mostly spending their cash on AI infrastructure instead.

"Nvidia is attractive on both a growth basis and a value basis, and it looks like a haven from any damage higher rates could do to the economy."

— Jim Awad, senior managing director at Clearstead Advisors

The second pillar is demand. Nvidia has guided to current-quarter revenue of about $108 billion, after last quarter's revenue roughly doubled from a year earlier. Supply-chain signals are firm: Taiwan's Foxconn reported record September revenue on AI server demand. And Morgan Stanley reinstated Nvidia as its top semiconductor pick after meetings with Huang, citing sustained AI demand, a broadening customer base and a valuation it considers relatively undemanding. The bank argued the main constraint on AI infrastructure is shifting from chip supply toward power and land for data centers — which could favor Nvidia as customers squeeze more computing output from limited electricity.

The comeback from March and July

The rally is striking given where the stock stood months ago. On March 30, the shares were down 11% for the year as investors questioned the hundreds of billions being spent on AI infrastructure. A July sell-off wiped around $1 trillion off the market value. Since then, sentiment has flipped: AI infrastructure spending looks entrenched, and inflation risks plus likely Fed rate hikes have made megacap tech look relatively safe.

"As rate hike fears have materialised money starts to move into these megacap tech stocks because they're a little bit more resistant to rate hikes," said Larry Tentarelli of Blue Chip Daily, adding that the semiconductor sector has also seen a rebound, with "big rotation back into semis, a big rotation back into the megacaps."

The skeptic's case: cheap for a reason

The numbers make Nvidia look paradoxically cheap: the stock trades at about 17 times earnings expected over the next 12 months, close to its lowest multiple in 10 years and a discount to the S&P 500, priced at 19 times forward earnings. Analysts project net income will double in fiscal 2027, which ends in January, with revenue leaping 90% — and the company previously projected sales expanding 70% in fiscal 2028, well above the 45% growth analysts had expected.

But there is a catch hiding in the record. Nvidia has been a laggard within its own sector this year: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is up 86% in 2026, with companies like Micron, Marvell and Intel up more than 200% even as they trade below their earlier record highs. A widely tracked semiconductor ETF is up about 96%, more than three times Nvidia's advance.

"Nvidia is a cheap stock, but the problem that Nvidia runs into, it's almost a victim of its own success. It just takes so much to move the needle."

— Larry Tentarelli, Blue Chip Daily

Part of the issue is physics: as the biggest stock in the world, it takes enormous buying to jolt shares that have been the S&P 500's best performers for a decade. Analysts remain divided on whether earnings growth can keep pushing the shares higher as the multiple compresses — and Deutsche Bank's research team has warned that stocks and bonds are pricing in irreconcilable economic worlds, one of which will have to yield.

What to watch

The next test is earnings against the $108 billion guide. Beyond that, the open questions are whether AI capital spending keeps broadening to new customers, whether the data-center bottleneck really shifts to power and land as Morgan Stanley argues, and how long the stock's valuation discount persists. Huang has said the company plans to double chip shipments in 2027 as data center construction accelerates — a promise the market will hold him to.
